title: Subresource Integrity
summary: Subresource integrity is a browser feature that lets a page declare a cryptographic hash for an external script or stylesheet, so the browser refuses to execute the file when its contents do not match that hash. The hash is written into the integrity attribute of the script or link element, normally alongside a crossorigin attribute so the browser can read a cross-origin response. It matters because most sites load code from content delivery networks and third party hosts, and a compromised or altered file would otherwise run with full page privileges in the user's session. The mistake people make is treating it as complete protection for third party code: it covers only elements that carry the attribute, it does nothing for dynamically injected or inline scripts, and every legitimate file update requires a new hash. Cross-origin resources also need suitable CORS headers or browsers will not perform the check.

beginner.definition: Subresource integrity is a safety check for files that a web page loads from another website. A hash is a short code calculated from the exact contents of a file. The page writes the expected code next to the link. If the file changes in any way, the codes no longer match and the browser refuses to use it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many websites load useful code from outside companies, such as fonts or design libraries. If that outside company is attacked, the attacker code runs inside your site. It could then steal what your users type. A hash check stops changed files before they run. It also catches files altered while travelling across the network. Without this check, your site trusts another company completely and cannot tell when that trust is abused.
howItWorks: The website owner calculates a hash of the exact file they intend to load.
They place that hash in the integrity attribute of the script or stylesheet tag.
When the page loads, the browser downloads the file and calculates the hash again.
The browser compares the two values, and the file runs only when they match.
If the file was changed or replaced, the values differ and the browser blocks it.
The owner must publish a new hash whenever they deliberately change that file.
beginner.example: Think of a parcel delivered to your flat by a courier you do not know. Before you accept it, you check a printed code against the code your friend sent you separately. If the codes match, the parcel is the one your friend posted. If they differ, something changed on the way and you send it back. Subresource integrity is that printed code for a web file, checked by the browser before the file is allowed in.
takeaways: Subresource integrity makes the browser verify a downloaded file before running it.
It only protects elements that carry the integrity attribute, so it is not a full answer for third party code.
Every time the file changes on purpose, the hash in your page must change too.

objectives: Explain what subresource integrity is and which problem it addresses.
Describe how a hash is used to verify a downloaded file.
Identify where the integrity attribute appears in a web page.
Explain the limits of this control for third party and dynamically loaded code.
Describe the maintenance work that a hash based check requires.
Explain why outside hosted code is a supply chain risk for a website.
